Bothies: Scotland's Free Mountain Shelters

Scattered across the Scottish Highlands and Islands, bothies are unlocked, unmanned shelters maintained by the Mountain Bothies Association (MBA). They're basic — stone walls, a roof, perhaps a fireplace — but they're free, atmospheric, and a uniquely Scottish experience for motorcycle tourers willing to venture off the beaten track.

What Is a Bothy?

Bothies are former shepherds' cottages, stalkers' lodges, or estate buildings that have been renovated to provide basic shelter for walkers, cyclists, and other outdoor enthusiasts. There are around 100 maintained bothies across Scotland, from the Borders to the far northwest.

Typical facilities include:

  • A solid roof and four walls (the basics, but crucial in Scottish weather)
  • A fireplace or wood-burning stove (bring your own fuel or collect fallen deadwood)
  • Sleeping platforms (wooden floors or platforms — bring your own sleeping bag and mat)
  • Sometimes a table and chairs
  • No electricity, running water, or toilet in most cases

Bothies Accessible by Motorcycle

Most bothies require a walk-in of 30 minutes to several hours, making them primarily a hillwalkers' resource. However, several are accessible from roads within a short walk:

  • Ryvoan Bothy, Cairngorms: 3-mile walk from Glenmore. Beautiful setting in ancient pine forest beside a green lochan.
  • Shenavall, Dundonnell: 6-mile walk but one of the most spectacular settings in Scotland, beneath An Teallach.
  • The Schoolhouse, Glen Feshie: Accessible via a track from the B970. A more comfortable bothy with a good stove.
  • Suardalan, Loch Hourn: Remote and atmospheric, accessed from the road end at Kinloch Hourn.

Bothy Etiquette

Bothies work because users respect a shared code of conduct:

  • Leave it cleaner than you found it. Carry out all your rubbish and sweep the floor before leaving.
  • Don't treat it as a hotel. Bothies are emergency shelters and shared spaces, not private accommodation.
  • No camping next to bothies. The MBA discourages camping within sight of a bothy — it's not a campsite.
  • Share the space. If others arrive, make room. Bothies are first-come, shared-use.
  • Respect the fire. Use the stove responsibly. Don't burn green wood or furniture.
  • Carry in, carry out. No waste, no food waste, no nothing left behind.
The bothy book is a treasured tradition. Most bothies have a logbook where visitors record their stay, the weather, and their adventures. Read the entries — they're often hilarious, poetic, or deeply moving. Add your own.

What to Bring for a Bothy Night

  • Sleeping bag (rated to at least 0°C for Scotland, even in summer)
  • Sleeping mat (bothy floors are hard and cold)
  • Head torch with spare batteries
  • Cooking stove and food (you can't rely on finding a stove or fuel)
  • Water purification (tablets or filter — bothy water sources are streams)
  • Firelighter and matches (if the bothy has a stove)
  • Rubbish bag (carry everything out)
  • A good book and a dram of whisky (optional but traditional)

Finding Bothies

The MBA doesn't publish exact coordinates to prevent overcrowding, but bothies are marked on Ordnance Survey maps and can be found through:

  • OS Maps (1:25000 and 1:50000 Explorer series)
  • The Mountain Bothies Association website (mountainbothies.org.uk)
  • Bothy-specific guidebooks
  • Online communities and forums

A bothy night is one of the great experiences of Scottish motorcycle touring. It's basic, it's sometimes cold, and it's always memorable. Even one night in a bothy will change how you think about accommodation forever.
keyTakeaways: Bothies are free, unlocked shelters maintained by the Mountain Bothies Association, with around 100 across Scotland.
Most need a walk-in of 30 minutes to several hours, but a few sit close to roads.
Facilities are basic: a roof, walls, sometimes a stove, and sleeping platforms; bring your own bag, mat and stove.
Follow bothy etiquette: leave it cleaner than you found it, carry everything out and share the space.
Find bothies via OS Maps and the MBA website; a sleeping bag rated to 0C is wise even in summer.

faq.a: A bothy is a former shepherd's cottage, stalker's lodge or estate building renovated to provide basic free shelter for walkers, cyclists and other outdoor users. Around 100 maintained bothies are scattered across Scotland, from the Borders to the far northwest, cared for by the Mountain Bothies Association.

faq.q: Can I reach bothies by motorcycle?
faq.a: Most bothies require a walk-in of 30 minutes to several hours, making them primarily a hillwalkers' resource, but several sit within a short walk of a road. Ryvoan Bothy is a 3-mile walk from Glenmore, The Schoolhouse in Glen Feshie is reached via a track from the B970, and Suardalan is accessed from the road end at Kinloch Hourn.

faq.q: What should I bring for a bothy night?
faq.a: Bring a sleeping bag rated to at least 0C for Scotland even in summer, a sleeping mat because floors are hard and cold, a head torch with spare batteries, a cooking stove and food since you cannot rely on finding fuel, water purification for stream sources, firelighters if there is a stove, and a rubbish bag to carry everything out.

faq.q: What is the bothy code of conduct?
faq.a: Leave the bothy cleaner than you found it and carry out all rubbish, do not treat it as a hotel or private accommodation, avoid camping within sight of it, share the space if others arrive since bothies are first-come and shared-use, use any stove responsibly without burning green wood or furniture, and leave nothing behind.

The MBA does not publish exact coordinates to prevent overcrowding, but bothies are marked on Ordnance Survey maps (the 1:25000 and 1:50000 Explorer series) and can be found through the Mountain Bothies Association website at mountainbothies.org.uk, bothy-specific guidebooks and online communities. Most also have a treasured logbook to read and sign.
